| Rank | Package | Latest version | GitHub project | Stars |
|---|---|---|---|---|

| 2 | @dumc11/tailwindcss | 0.4.0 | tailwindcss/tailwindcss | 73,464 |

| 5 | @dothq/styled-components | 1.0.0 | styled-components/styled-components | 39,660 |

Ranks 4 and 5 are tied, so both are included. The 6th place is @ec-nordbund/leaflet (1.7.1, 38,715 stars).

How I got there:
- **Latest release:** For each NPM package name, I kept only versions with `IsRelease: true` and took the one with the highest `Ordinal`. Using the latest upstream publish time instead gives the same top 5.
- **Join:** I matched `System`, `Name`, and `Version` to `project_packageversion`, keeping only `ProjectType = GITHUB`, then matched `ProjectName` to the repo named in `project_info`.
- **Stars:** `project_info` has no key column, so I parsed the `owner/repo` name and the star count from the `Project_Information` text. That covered 617 repositories.

Two caveats. The package names look unusual (for example, @dylanvann/svelte maps to sveltejs/svelte), but the mapping comes straight from the `project_packageversion` table. The ranking covers only packages whose GitHub project appears in `project_info` with a parseable star count, so a package whose repository isn't in that table can't rank.

The top 5 NPM MIT projects with release versions by GitHub fork count are:

| Rank | Project | Forks | Stars |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | semantic-org/semantic-ui | 4,955 | not parsed |
| 2 | react-native-community/react-native-webview | 2,962 | 6,345 |
| 3 | sass/node-sass | 1,326 | 8,498 |
| 4 | mbrn/material-table | 1,035 | 3,464 |
| 5 | thejameskyle/react-loadable | 857 | 16,576 |

The stars column is shown for completeness. It was not part of the ranking.

**How I got there**
- **Release packages:** I kept NPM rows in `packageinfo` whose `VersionInfo` has `"IsRelease": true`, giving 166,288 distinct (Name, Version) pairs.
- **Package-to-project link:** I joined those pairs to `project_packageversion` on Name and Version.
- **Project record:** I took the repo from the `"The project <owner/repo> ..."` prefix of `project_info.Project_Information` and matched it to `ProjectName`, ignoring case.
- **MIT filter:** I kept projects whose `project_info.Licenses` contains "MIT".
- **Fork count:** I parsed the number before "forks" in `Project_Information`.

This leaves 357 MIT projects with a release package. I ranked them by fork count and kept the top 5.

**Caveats**
- 111 of the 652 `project_info` descriptions did not follow the "The project …" pattern, so I could not parse a repo name from them. If any of those are MIT-licensed NPM projects with high fork counts, they are missing from the ranking.
- The `semantic-ui` fork count of 4,955 is what the database says, but I did not check it against GitHub.

Among non-Python repositories, about **16.8%** of their README.md files include copyright information (17 of 101).

**How I got there**

- **Non-Python repos:** I treated a repo as non-Python if its `language_description` does not mention Python. That gives 2.77M repos in the `languages` table, which I joined to the artifacts data by repo name.
- **README files:** I used `contents` rows where `sample_path = 'README.md'` (exact case) in those repos. This gave 101 files across these repos.
- **Copyright:** a file counts if its content contains "copyright" (case-insensitive) or the © symbol. Fifteen match the word "copyright" and two match only ©.

**Sensitivity to choices**

| Definition | Files | With copyright | Proportion |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exact `README.md`, includes repos with no language info (main answer) | 101 | 17 | 16.8% |
| Exact `README.md`, excludes repos with no language info | 95 | 17 | 17.9% |
| Case-insensitive `readme.md` | 105 | 18 | 17.1% |

The answer is roughly 17–18% under any reasonable variant. I used the main definition because repos with no language information still don't declare Python.

For LGG patients, the average log10(normalized_count + 1) of IGF2 expression by histology type is:

| Histological type | Mean log10(IGF2 + 1) | Patients |
|---|---|---|
| Astrocytoma | 2.5713 (2.571298) | 10 |
| Oligoastrocytoma | 2.7136 (2.713571) | 5 |
| Oligodendroglioma | 2.6825 (2.682458) | 8 |

Across all 23 patients the overall mean is 2.6409.

Each of the 23 patients has one IGF2 sample, so using all samples or only primary tumor (TP) samples gives identical results.

Method:
- **Cohort:** The clinical table has no cancer-type column, so I took LGG to mean the 513 patients whose `Patient_description` names "Brain lower grade glioma". I pulled each TCGA barcode from that text with a regex and matched it to `ParticipantBarcode`.
- **Filters:** I kept only patients with a non-null IGF2 `normalized_count` and a histology annotation not in square brackets. No LGG rows had bracketed values, so that filter removed nothing.
- **Transformation:** I computed log10(normalized_count + 1) per sample, then averaged within each histology type.

The 23 matched patients are a small slice of the 513 LGG patients, because most LGG patients have no IGF2 expression row in the RNA-seq table.

The query returns four citing patents from three assignees, plus one individual holder. Each subclass has a single official title in the CPC dump.

| Citing assignee | Primary CPC subclass | Full subclass title |
|---|---|---|
| CALIFORNIA INST OF TECHN | G01V | GEOPHYSICS; GRAVITATIONAL MEASUREMENTS; DETECTING MASSES OR OBJECTS; TAGS |
| BLOOM ENERGY CORP | H01M | PROCESSES OR MEANS, e.g. BATTERIES, FOR THE DIRECT CONVERSION OF CHEMICAL ENERGY INTO ELECTRICAL ENERGY |
| CRYSTAL IS INC | C30B | SINGLE-CRYSTAL GROWTH; UNIDIRECTIONAL SOLIDIFICATION OF EUTECTIC MATERIAL OR UNIDIRECTIONAL DEMIXING OF EUTECTOID MATERIAL; REFINING BY ZONE-MELTING OF MATERIAL; PRODUCTION OF A HOMOGENEOUS POLYCRYSTALLINE MATERIAL WITH DEFINED STRUCTURE; SINGLE CRYSTALS OR HOMOGENEOUS POLYCRYSTALLINE MATERIAL WITH DEFINED STRUCTURE; AFTER-TREATMENT OF SINGLE CRYSTALS OR A HOMOGENEOUS POLYCRYSTALLINE MATERIAL WITH DEFINED STRUCTURE; APPARATUS THEREFOR |
| SCHOWALTER LEO J (individual holder) | H01L | SEMICONDUCTOR DEVICES NOT COVERED BY CLASS H10 |

**Details**

- **CALIFORNIA INST OF TECHN** cites US-6237292-B1. Its primary CPC is G01V1/01.
- **BLOOM ENERGY CORP** cites US-6767662-B2. Its primary CPCs are H01M4/9066 and H01M8/2425.
- **CRYSTAL IS INC** cites US-2010025717-A1. Its primary CPCs are C30B11/003, C30B25/10 and C30B25/16.
- **SCHOWALTER LEO J** cites US-2010025717-A1. Its primary CPC is H01L21/0262. This is an individual, not a company, so you may not want it counted as an assignee.

**Method**

- I identified the 169 UNIV CALIFORNIA patents from their `Patents_info` text. Then I matched their publication numbers against the `publication_number` entries in every patent's `citation` list. All citation JSON parsed, so no matches were skipped.
- The assignee names come from the `Patents_info` sentence for each citing patent.
- I took the subclass from the `first = true` CPC entries and mapped it to its four-character symbol.
- The titles come from the `titleFull` field of the CPC dump. The live Postgres socket wasn't available, so I read the bundled `patent_CPCDefinition.sql` file directly.

- **Reports dated on or before 2023-01-01:** I excluded rid_0001 (Sept 2023), rid_0004 (June 2023), and rid_0014 (March 2023). The other 16 agendas are dated 2021–2022, and their in-text dates agree.
- **Status:** Each project's status comes from the section heading it sits under. For each project I took its most recent report on or before the cutoff. Corral Canyon Road Bridge Repairs is listed as "Design" in the latest report (rid_0019), so it is out.
- **Entity resolution:** The guardrail project appears in the funding table as `guardrail_replacement_citywide`, `guardrail_replacement_citywide_fema_project`, and `guardrail_replacement_citywide_fema_caloes_project`. These are the same project under different names. Its last agenda mention (rid_0015, Dec 2021) lists it as "Completed". All 24 grants for these names are dated on or before 2021-11-23, so all count toward the total.
- **Runners-up:** Corral Canyon Culvert Repairs about $13.46M, Birdview Avenue Improvements about $12.68M, Storm Drain Trash Screens $11.49M. Civic Center Way, Civic Center Stormwater Diversion, Malibu Park Storm Drain Repairs, the 2021 Annual Street Maintenance, and Dume Drive speed humps are all lower.

One judgment call: the agendas list "Citywide Guardrail Replacement" and "Guardrail Replacement Citywide (FEMA Project)" separately in the same agenda (rid_0010), so I treated them as distinct projects. That keeps `citywide_guardrail_replacement` ($2,295,000) out of the total. If it were merged in, the total would be $35,712,000, but the project would still be the same.

**Answer: 2023, with $61,179,000 in capital project funding.**

Capital projects received more funding in 2023 than in any other year. The 2022 total was $41,714,000 and 2021 was $21,467,000. No funding records in the data fall in 2020 with a prior report, so 2020 has no capital total.

How I got there:
- **Agendas:** I decoded the 19 BSON agendas and used each report's meeting date. The header, "Date prepared" and "Meeting date" agree everywhere except rid_0010. Its text describes the January 20, 2022 meeting as already held and the January 24, 2022 meeting as upcoming, so I treated it as about January 21, 2022. - **Entity resolution:** I grouped funding names that differ only by agency suffixes (`_fema_project`, `_caloes_project`, `_caljpia_project`, and combinations) and matched them to agenda titles. I excluded the two noise names, `discussion` and `recommended_action`.
- **Type:** For each funding record, I took the section of the most recent report on or before its grant date. Records whose project appears in no such report (391 of 746) are left out, since their type is undefined.
- **Mixed sections:** Reports rid_0001 and rid_0004 list projects under "Capital Improvement and Disaster Recovery Projects", which doesn't say whether they are capital or disaster. I used each project's type from its most recent non-mixed listing. In rid_0014, several of these projects appear under capital. Only Outdoor Warning Sirens resolves to disaster. Its 2023 records ($538,000) are excluded.

The 2023 figure depends on how the mixed-section projects are classified. Counting all of them as capital gives $61,717,000. **005Wt000003NJgAIAW**

This is Priya Choudhury's User Id. Across the three agents with April 2023 opportunities that have matched contracts, she had the shortest average cycle, 49 days from opportunity creation to contract company-signed date. The other two averaged 168 days (`005Wt000003NEa3IAG`) and 186 days (`005Wt000003NISMIA4`).

Her average rests on a single opportunity, so the margin is based on one deal each. I stripped leading `#` and surrounding whitespace before joining, and I matched Opportunity.ContractID__c to Contract.Id and grouped by Opportunity.OwnerId. The User table stores her Id without the `#` prefix.

This is the order owner (`Order.OwnerId`) with the highest total of Quantity × UnitPrice across orders whose linked contract has a CompanySignedDate between 2022-06-25 and 2022-11-25 (roughly the past five months from 2022-11-25). Total for this agent: about 96,136.

- **Join path:** `Order` has no direct link to `Opportunity` or `Contract`, so I joined on account (`Order.AccountId` to the contract's AccountId). Orders were included when the account had a contract signed in the window.
- **Agent definition:** I credited the order's owner rather than the opportunity's owner. Opportunity-owner attribution gives a different top agent (`005Wt000003NBp4IAG`), so this choice matters.

I normalised IDs by stripping leading `#` and surrounding whitespace before joining. The returned Id is the clean form; the User table stores it as `#005Wt000003NHw5IAG`, which is the same record.

- **The ranking depends on how vague prose is treated.** If vague rows count as under $1M, Homeland Security leads (31.2% vs. Veterans Affairs at 25.3%). If they count as over $1M, Veterans Affairs edges ahead (42.3% vs. 42.0%) and the Department of the Interior tops the list.
- **Restricting to exact numbers doesn't settle it.** Only 2 of Environmental Protection Agency's 16 contracts have exact figures, so the numeric-only ranking is driven by tiny samples.

**Method**

1. **Contracts → amounts.** Award ids were normalized (strip separators, uppercase, undo OCR confusions). Canonical ids were taken from `generated_internal_id`, since they are cleaner. About 1,300 amount rows still match two or more contracts that differ only by OCR-confusable characters (e.g. B vs 8), so they were left out.
2. **Agencies.** `awarding_agency` was mapped to canonical names via `agency_aliases`. There are 22 agencies with at least 10 contracts.
3. **Amount classification.** Exact numbers were compared to $1,000,000 directly. Prose was classified by its magnitude band: seven-figure, millions, and tens of millions count as over $1M; five/six-figure, thousands, and "under a million" count as under.
4. **Result (explicit bands only).** Homeland Security: 86 of 246 classifiable contracts (35.0%). Veterans Affairs was next at 30.5%.

**How I got it**
- I loaded the Postgres dump (`contracts.sql`) into an in-memory SQLite database. The `award_id` values match exactly between `contracts` and `contract_amounts` for all 9,921 awards, so no fuzzy resolution was needed. I didn't query the live Postgres server.
- I normalized each `naics_code` by stripping the `naics-` prefix and separators and mapping OCR letters to digits. Every code normalized to 6 digits, and the sectors match the `naics_sectors` reference table in `agencies.duckdb`.
- I parsed the exact amount formats present (plain numbers, `$x,xxx.xx`, `x USD`, `xK`, `xM`). Then I kept awards with an exact amount ≥ $10,000,000 and counted distinct sectors.

**Caveat on coverage**
- Only 517 of 9,921 awards have an exact numeric amount in `contract_amounts`. The other ~9,400 rows are prose such as "eight-figure commitment" or "low-to-mid millions", which don't give an exact figure.
- The prose is also unreliable. For example, one award has an exact value of 1.1M but is described as "six-figure", and another with an exact value of 8.6M is labeled "eight-figure".
- If I used the prose magnitude bands that clearly mean ≥ $10M ("eight-figure", "nine-figure", "ten-figure", "tens of millions") as well, the count rises to 11 sectors. That figure is a rough estimate, not a verified result. I reported the exact-value answer because it is the only one the data supports directly.

**57** distinct recipients (canonical names) are each associated with more than one UEI.

I grouped the 3,317 rows by normalized name and counted the groups with more than one normalized UEI. Two normalizations were applied:

- **UEIs:** stripped the `uei:` prefix and `-uei` suffix, uppercased, and folded the OCR-confusable characters to one form. This kept all 3,317 UEIs distinct, so nothing was wrongly merged.
- **Names:** uppercased, removed punctuation, and dropped trailing corporate suffixes (Inc, LLC, Corp, Co, Ltd, and so on). Examples of what this merges: "LOCKHEED MARTIN CORP." with "Lockheed Martin Corporation", and "AIRGAS USA, L.L.C" with "AIRGAS USA LLC.".

A looser key that also drops a leading "THE" and all spaces produces the same 57 groups, so the result doesn't depend on how strict the name matching is. The largest groups are RAYTHEON (8 UEIs), NORTHROP GRUMMAN SYSTEMS (8), LOCKHEED MARTIN (8) and THE BOEING (7).
